A logistic item response model is a very small neural network. The Rasch model
takes a person, looks up one number for them ($\theta_p$), takes an item, looks
up one number for it ($b_i$), subtracts, and passes the difference through a
sigmoid. In PyTorch terms that is two `nn.Embedding` layers and no hidden
layer. The 2PL adds a second item lookup (the slope $a_i$). Once the models are
written this way it is natural to ask what happens when the network is made
wider or deeper: more latent dimensions, a nonlinear decoder. Does a neural
network predict item responses better than the 2PL?

This page builds the classical models in PyTorch, checks that they recover what
the `mirt` package recovers, widens them, and scores every model on held-out
responses from five IRW tables with the [InterModel Vigorish (IMV)](imv.qmd).
Two more flexible one-dimensional models from R's `mirt` (the monotonic
polynomial and an asymmetric item curve) are fit offline on the same split and
join the comparison.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup"
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import irw
from nn_irt_helpers import (TABLES, prepare, fit, predict, imv, log_loss,
                            make_models, SEED)

Rasch, TwoPL, Bilinear, MLP = make_models()
torch.set_num_threads(4)
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110
```

## The models, written as networks

The four model classes below are the whole of the modelling code. Each takes a
batch of person indices and item indices and returns a logit.

| Model | Person lookup | Item lookup | Combine |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rasch | $\theta_p$ (1 number) | $b_i$ (1 number) | $\theta_p - b_i$ |
| 2PL | $\theta_p$ (1) | $a_i, b_i$ (2) | $a_i(\theta_p - b_i)$ |
| MIRT, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf a_i$ ($k$), $b_i$ | $\mathbf a_i \cdot \boldsymbol\theta_p - b_i$ |
| MLP, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf v_i$ ($k$) | $\mathrm{MLP}([\boldsymbol\theta_p, \mathbf v_i])$ |

The MIRT model is the compensatory multidimensional 2PL: $k$-dimensional
person and item embeddings combined by a dot product, which is also a low-rank
matrix factorisation of the logit matrix. With $k=1$ it is the 2PL; the page
uses $k=2$. The MLP concatenates the two embeddings and passes them through
hidden layers of ReLU units, so the interaction between person and item is no
longer constrained to be a dot product. This is the shape used in neural
collaborative filtering. Two sizes are fit, both on $k=2$ embeddings: a small
one with a single hidden layer of 16 units, and a large one with two hidden
layers of 64, so that depth is the only thing that changes.

```{python}
import inspect
print(inspect.getsource(Rasch))
print(inspect.getsource(TwoPL))
```

The full source of all four, and of the training loop, is in
[`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py).

## Held-out cells, not held-out people

Every one of these models has a parameter per person. A model cannot predict a
person it has never seen, so the usual split by rows (train on some people,
test on others) is impossible. Instead we hold out **cells**: 20% of each
person's responses, chosen at random, are hidden during training and predicted
afterwards. Every person and every item stays in the training set. The same
mask is used by every model, including the `mirt` fits, which see the held-out
cells as missing.

The tables are all dense and dichotomous. They were chosen to vary in size and
in how much structure beyond a single dimension there is to find. Tables with
more than 5,000 respondents or 116 items are subsampled to those caps (fixed
seed) so that every fit on the page stays small; the sizes below are the
originals.

| Table | What it is | Persons x items |
|---|---|---|
| `borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt` | Brazilian medical residency entrance exam, computer-based form | 3,223 x 120 |
| `encceja_2024_ef_lp` | Brazilian adult-education certification exam, Portuguese (INEP) | 23,462 x 30 |
| `psychoneurotic_inventory` | Woodworth Psychoneurotic Inventory, yes/no symptom items | 6,019 x 116 |
| `cdm_ecpe` | ECPE grammar test with a known three-attribute Q-matrix | 2,922 x 28 |
| `art` | Author Recognition Test, native and non-native readers | 1,402 x 50 |

```{python}
data = {t: prepare(t) for t in TABLES}
pd.DataFrame({t: {"persons": int(d.pid.max() + 1), "items": int(d.iid.max() + 1),
                  "train cells": int((~d.test).sum()), "test cells": int(d.test.sum()),
                  "mean resp": round(float(d.resp.mean()), 3)}
              for t, d in data.items()}).T.astype({"persons": int, "items": int,
                                                     "train cells": int, "test cells": int})
```

`prepare` calls `irw.fetch`, caches the table, subsamples, assigns integer
indices, and draws the mask with a fixed seed.

## Rasch and 2PL in PyTorch

Training is minibatch Adam on the binary cross-entropy of the training cells.
One detail matters: fitting a free parameter per person by maximum likelihood
is **joint** maximum likelihood, which is inconsistent as the number of persons
grows and overfits persons with extreme scores. Adding an L2 penalty on the
person embedding is the same as putting a normal prior on $\theta$, so the
estimate is a MAP estimate and close to what `mirt` returns from marginal
maximum likelihood. The `person_decay` argument sets that penalty.

```{python}
d = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"]
n_p, n_i = d.pid.max() + 1, d.iid.max() + 1
rasch, h_rasch = fit(Rasch(n_p, n_i), d, epochs=30)
twopl, h_2pl = fit(TwoPL(n_p, n_i), d, epochs=30)
h_rasch.tail(1), h_2pl.tail(1)
```

Does the network recover the item parameters? Fit the same two models with the
Python `mirt` package (marginal maximum likelihood on the training cells) and
compare.

```{python}
from mirt import fit_mirt
wide = d[~d.test].pivot(index="pid", columns="iid", values="resp")
wide_arr = wide.to_numpy(dtype=float).copy()
wide_arr[np.isnan(wide_arr)] = -1
wide_arr = wide_arr.astype(int)
m_rasch = fit_mirt(wide_arr, model="1PL")
m_2pl = fit_mirt(wide_arr, model="2PL")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))
b_nn = rasch.b.weight.detach().numpy().ravel()
b_nn = b_nn - b_nn.mean()
ax[0].scatter(m_rasch.model.difficulty - m_rasch.model.difficulty.mean(), b_nn, s=12)
ax[0].set(xlabel="mirt Rasch difficulty", ylabel="PyTorch Rasch difficulty")
a_nn = np.exp(twopl.log_a.weight.detach().numpy().ravel())
ax[1].scatter(m_2pl.model.discrimination, a_nn, s=12)
ax[1].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL discrimination", ylabel="PyTorch 2PL discrimination")
for a in ax:
    lo, hi = a.get_xlim(); a.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], "k--", lw=0.8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The gradient-descent fits land where the marginal-likelihood fits land. The
Rasch difficulties are centred before plotting because the location of
$\theta$ is not identified in the network (there is no prior mean), and the
discriminations sit a little above the line because the person prior shrinks
the $\theta$ estimates to a variance below one, and the slopes stretch to
compensate; the ordering of items is the same.

## Widening the network

Now the models that are not classical IRT. Train-versus-test log-loss by epoch
makes the overfitting visible: once the test curve turns up, further training
is memorising the training cells.

```{python}
curves = {}
curves["Rasch"] = h_rasch
curves["2PL"] = h_2pl
_, curves["MIRT k=2"] = fit(Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2), d, epochs=30)
_, curves["MLP small"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)), d, epochs=30)
_, curves["MLP large"] = fit(MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)), d, epochs=30)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharey=False)
for name, h in curves.items():
    ax[0].plot(h.epoch, h.train, label=name)
    ax[1].plot(h.epoch, h.test, label=name)
ax[0].set(title="training log-loss", xlabel="epoch", ylabel="log-loss")
ax[1].set(title="held-out log-loss", xlabel="epoch")
ax[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Scoring with the IMV

The IMV converts a log-loss improvement into a bet: if model 0 predicts
held-out responses as well as a coin with bias $w_0$ and model 1 as well as a
coin with bias $w_1$, the IMV is $(w_1 - w_0)/w_0$, the relative gain in the
bettor's edge. The [IMV vignette](imv.qmd) has the definition and the R
package; here it is in Python.

```{python}
print(inspect.getsource(imv))
```

Fit every model on every table. Each PyTorch model is trained for a fixed
budget of epochs with the epoch of lowest held-out loss reported (early
stopping, with the held-out set doing double duty as validation set; a
production comparison would carve a third split). The `mirt` fits come from
[`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R),
run offline on the same split.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Fit all PyTorch models on all tables"
from pathlib import Path

def best_epoch_preds(model_fn, d, epochs=30):
    """Train, keep the predictions from the epoch with lowest held-out loss."""
    te = d[d.test]
    best = (np.inf, None)
    model = model_fn()
    hist = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model, h = fit(model, d, epochs=1, seed=SEED + ep)
        p = predict(model, te)
        ll = log_loss(te.resp.values, p)
        hist.append(ll)
        if ll < best[0]:
            best = (ll, p)
    return best[1]

nn_specs = {
    "Rasch": lambda n_p, n_i: Rasch(n_p, n_i),
    "2PL": lambda n_p, n_i: TwoPL(n_p, n_i),
    "MIRT k=2": lambda n_p, n_i: Bilinear(n_p, n_i, 2),
    "MLP small": lambda n_p, n_i: MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(16,)),
    "MLP large": lambda n_p, n_i: MLP(n_p, n_i, 2, hidden=(64, 64)),
}
preds = {}
for t, d in data.items():
    n_p, n_i = d.pid.max() + 1, d.iid.max() + 1
    te = d[d.test]
    preds[t] = {"y": te.resp.values}
    for name, mk in nn_specs.items():
        preds[t][name] = best_epoch_preds(lambda: mk(n_p, n_i), d)
    mp = Path("nn_irt_data") / f"{t}_mirt_preds.csv.gz"
    if mp.exists():
        m = pd.read_csv(mp, dtype={"id": str, "item": str})
        m = te[["id", "item"]].merge(m, on=["id", "item"], how="left")
        for c in m.columns:
            if c.startswith("mirt_"):
                preds[t][c] = m[c].values
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "IMV table"
rows = []
for t, pr in preds.items():
    y = pr["y"]
    base = pr["2PL"]
    for name, p in pr.items():
        if name == "y" or np.isnan(p).all():
            continue
        rows.append({"table": t, "model": name,
                     "log-loss": log_loss(y, p),
                     "IMV vs 2PL": imv(y, base, p),
                     "IMV vs Rasch": imv(y, pr["Rasch"], p)})
res = pd.DataFrame(rows)
tab = res.pivot(index="model", columns="table", values="IMV vs 2PL")
tab = tab.reindex([m for m in list(nn_specs) + ["mirt_2pl", "mirt_monopoly", "mirt_lpe"]
                   if m in tab.index])[TABLES]
tab.round(4).style.format("{:+.4f}", na_rep="").background_gradient(cmap="RdBu", vmin=-0.05, vmax=0.05, axis=None)
```

Positive values mean the model predicts held-out responses better than the
PyTorch 2PL on that table; the 2PL row is zero by construction. The `mirt_`
rows are R's `mirt` fit by marginal maximum likelihood on the same training
cells, with each held-out cell predicted by its posterior-predictive
probability (the item curve integrated over the person's posterior): the 2PL
again, as the marginal-likelihood anchor for the PyTorch 2PL; the monotonic
polynomial model, whose item curve is a flexible monotone function rather than
a logistic; and the logistic positive exponent model (LPE), whose item curve
is asymmetric. The last two change the *shape* of the item curve while keeping
one latent dimension, which is the opposite move from the networks above.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Held-out log-loss"
res.pivot(index="model", columns="table", values="log-loss").reindex(tab.index)[TABLES].round(4)
```

Three things stand out.

**On the cognitive tests the 2PL is the model to beat, and nothing beats it.**
On the residency exam, ENCCEJA and the ECPE grammar test every network is at
or below the 2PL. The two-dimensional MIRT is the worst offender: with only 30
or 28 items per person its second dimension is fitted to noise, and early
stopping cannot save it. The MLPs lose less, because their decoder is
regularised by the same person prior and their extra capacity goes unused, but
they do not gain. The ECPE result is the instructive one: the test has a known
three-attribute structure, and a model built to find structure still does not
predict better, because the attributes are so highly correlated that one
dimension carries them.

**Where the nets win, it is multidimensionality, and the MIRT finds it as well
as the MLP.** On the Woodworth inventory, 116 yes/no symptom items spanning
several syndromes, the two-dimensional MIRT beats the 2PL by about the same
margin the 2PL beats Rasch. On the Author Recognition Test the gain is smaller
and comes from a known second dimension, native versus non-native readers.
In both cases the MLPs match or trail the MIRT: once the embeddings are
two-dimensional, a nonlinear decoder adds nothing, and the large MLP is never
better than the small one. Depth is not where the signal is.

**Part of the apparent gain is estimation, not model.** The `mirt_2pl` row is
the same 2PL as the PyTorch one and should sit at zero. It does not: marginal
maximum likelihood with posterior-predictive held-out probabilities beats the
MAP point estimates by a small margin on every table and by a noticeable one
on the Woodworth, where persons have 116 responses and extreme score patterns.
So the fair comparison for the networks is against the PyTorch 2PL (same
estimator) and the fair comparison for the flexible item curves is against
`mirt_2pl`. On that reading, the monotonic polynomial and the asymmetric LPE
curve add almost nothing to the 2PL on any table (and the polynomial did not
converge on the two 116-item tables), while the MIRT's gain on the Woodworth
survives the estimation correction with roughly half its size. The page could
close the estimator gap by integrating the networks' predictions over a person
posterior too; that is a variational IRT, which is where the closing section
points.

## What this page does not do

The networks here see only person and item identities, exactly as the
classical models do, so this is a comparison of functional forms, not of
information. Models that use more information are a different question:
sequential models of learning (knowledge tracing) use the order of responses;
models with item text as input can predict items never seen in training;
variational IRT replaces the point estimates with an encoder network that
amortises person scoring. All of them can be scored with the same held-out
cells and the same IMV.
